# Deep Learning Fundamentals: Optimization, Drift, Calibration

[← NVIDIA](../README.md) · [Every NVIDIA question](../../nvidia.md) · [Read it on TrueInterview](https://trueinterview.io/study/deep-learning-fundamentals)

`calibration` `distribution` `ml-knowledge` `optimization`

---

## Requirements

Be ready to explain and reason through each of the following without writing code:

- The mechanics of gradient descent and the purpose of the learning rate.
- Whether gradient descent is assured of finding a global optimum.
- The types of loss surfaces that ensure convergence to a global minimum.
- The pros and cons of full-batch, mini-batch, and stochastic gradient descent.
- The distinction between bias and variance, along with ways to reduce each one.
- Why small batches may move out of sharp or shallow local minima.
- The generalization gap between the training distribution and the population distribution.
- Why flatter minima can produce better generalization than sharp minima.
- What confidence calibration means and which methods are commonly used.
- What model drift is and how it can be identified.
- How to convert a customer or business situation into an ML problem with measurable outcomes.

## Notes

The responses should be conceptual while remaining technically exact.

- Convex loss landscapes are the straightforward case: every local minimum is also global.
- Compared with full-batch GD, SGD produces noisier gradient estimates, and that randomness can help it leave certain sharp or shallow basins.
- Full-batch optimization calculates the exact empirical gradient, but it can settle in sharper minima and is frequently harder to scale.
- A generalization gap occurs when training loss and population loss separate; flatter minima are less affected by minor shifts in the data distribution.
- Calibration concerns whether predicted probabilities correspond to observed frequencies. Common techniques include temperature scaling, Platt scaling, isotonic regression, and reliability diagrams.
- Drift monitoring may track changes in feature distributions, prediction distributions, calibration, performance once delayed labels arrive, and business KPI differences.

## Preparation

- Sketch three loss landscapes: a convex bowl, a sharp minimum, and a flat minimum.
- Rehearse a 90-second explanation of how mini-batch noise may help leave sharp minima while making convergence less steady.
- Practice describing batch-size trade-offs without vaguely attributing everything to “noise.”
- Develop one business scenario in which a customer sees poorer model decisions after deployment; connect it to a drift, calibration, or data-quality investigation.
